title: Hudson Taylor
hook: an English missionary in China puts on Chinese clothes, grows the braid, and learns the dialects

segments.voice: Yesterday: William Booth's Salvation Army, its brass bands, its uniforms and its pot of soup. Your line was soup, soap, salvation.

A barber's razor scrapes across the front of a young Englishman's head. The hair at the back is left to grow, so it can be braided into a long queue, the way Chinese men wore it then. He folds away his European suit and puts on the loose robe and cloth shoes of a Chinese teacher. Other foreigners in the port city laugh at him. Some missionaries are embarrassed for him. A few are angry: he's letting the side down. His name is Hudson Taylor, and if he's going to live among the people of China, he's going to stop looking like a visitor.

The first change was the map. Taylor wanted to go beyond the port cities, inland, to provinces far from the sea. So he founded the China Inland Mission, and asked those who joined to dress as he did, learn the local dialects, and live simply among their neighbors. The reason he gave was Paul, in the King James Bible: "I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some." Taylor applied it to his wardrobe. If a foreign suit was a wall, he would take it off. Christians say God did this first. John's Gospel says: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." In Christian belief, God didn't shout from a distance; he came close, in a body, a language, a place. Some readers see Taylor's clothes and dialects as a small echo of that. Then the harder part, from day nine hundred seventeen and Ramabai: the honest history of missions. Taylor came to China in an age of empire, when Western powers had used force to open China's ports, and opium was part of that trade. Taylor spoke out against the opium trade, and wanted the gospel to look Chinese rather than British. But he was still a foreigner, and the clothes didn't change that. In time, Chinese Christians led their own churches, and they hold a range of views about the missionary era. The idea Taylor reached for was simple and costly: don't ask people to become like you. Become one of them, as far as love can take you.
screen: `STILL A FOREIGNER IN AN EMPIRE AGE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone near you whose culture isn't yours: a neighbor, a coworker, the family who runs the corner shop. Think about what you actually know of their ways, a greeting, a holiday, a food, and notice how little, or how much. If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, hold them in mind with real interest.
Hudson Taylor. An English missionary who put on Chinese clothes, learned the dialects and went inland, beyond the port cities.
Your line: become one of them. Love learns another's way before explaining its own. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Christian mission agencies today ask workers to learn the local language and culture deeply before anything else, and churches in China are led by Chinese Christians.

fork.setup: you've just arrived in China. the other foreigners wear European suits and stay near the ports. what do you do?
options: keep your suit. you're English, after all.
wear Chinese clothes, learn the dialects and go inland.
stay at the port and wait for people to come to you.
fork.reveal: Taylor changed his clothes, his hair and his language, and went inland. other foreigners laughed. he went anyway.

trapdoor: what you thought: a missionary in fancy dress.
what it means: a man who changed his clothes, hair and language to live among the people he served, instead of asking them to become like him.
what a scholar hears: Paul's "all things to all men," rooted in John's "the Word was made flesh," practiced by a foreigner who still lived inside an age of empire.

chat.says: Why did Hudson Taylor shave his head and wear Chinese clothes?
options: To stop looking like a visitor: all things to all men, so his clothes weren't a wall.
Because British officials ordered every missionary in China to dress that way.
As a costume for a festival, and then he found it comfortable and kept it.
chat.meaning: Taylor applied Paul's all things to all men to his wardrobe: if a foreign suit was a wall between him and his neighbors, he took it off.

queue.meaning: a long braid worn by Chinese men at that time

China Inland Mission.meaning: Taylor's mission to China's provinces far from the coast

opium.meaning: a drug whose trade was forced on China in that age

the Word was made flesh.meaning: John's words for God coming close, in Jesus's own body
